shipped.title_o: Automaticity of social behavior: Direct effects of trait construct and stereotype activation on action.
shipped.outcome_quote: First, in Experiment 1, despite the use of a larger sample and an experimental procedure devoid of the limitations present in the original experiment, we were not able to replicate Bargh et al’s [1] automatic effect of priming on walking speed.

blind_target.authors: Bargh JA, Chen M, Burrows L
blind_target.title: Automaticity of social behavior: direct effects of trait construct and stereotype-activation on action.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
Here, we sought to replicate Bargh et al's
[1]
experiments.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Despite the use of automated timing methods and a larger sample, our first experiment failed to show priming. Our second experiment was aimed at manipulating the beliefs of the experimenters: Half were led to think that participants would walk slower when primed congruently, and the other half was led to expect the opposite. Strikingly, we obtained a walking speed effect, but only when experimenters believed participants would indeed walk slower.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly report failure in Experiment 1 and conditional replication in Experiment 2, including objective timings. The paper questions automaticity, awareness and expectancy but does not give an overall verdict that overrides its opposing study results; aggregate mixed rather than treating one condition as the whole attempt.

items.parent_scope_question: Parent unresolved scope question: does experimenter-expectancy critique constitute the main methodological invalidity message, requiring statistically successful but flawed, or do authors present ordinary mixed replication? Apply special verdict and overall priority rules using authors own account.

blind_target.title: The chameleon effect: The perception–behavior link and social interaction.
blind_target.evidence_quote: In the context of this bachelor thesis, I attempted a close replication of Chartrand and Bargh’s experiment 1.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The results of the experiment overall do not suffice to meet my preset criterion of a successful replication, which was defined in the preregistration document of the experiment and is available via the Open Science Framework.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Rule 1: the author explicitly judges the experiment overall not to meet the preset successful-replication criterion. Low power is discussed as a limitation but not as an overall inability to adjudicate.

shipped.title_o: An inkblot for attitudes: Affect misattribution as implicit measurement.
shipped.outcome_quote: We find that although the average AMP effect remains positive, it decreases significantly in magnitude. Moreover, this reduction in the mean AMP effect under incentives masks large heterogeneity: one subset of individuals continues to experience the ‘full’ AMP effect, while another reduces their effect to approximately zero.

blind_target.authors: Payne, B. K., Cheng, C. M., Govorun, O., & Stewart, B. D.
blind_target.title: An inkblot for attitudes: Affect misattribution as implicit measurement
blind_target.evidence_quote: Our implementation of the AMP closely follows experiments 1-4 of Payne et al. (2005).
blind_target.outcome_quote: Our results first replicate key findings of Payne et al. (2005): we show that warning participants about the effect of the prime on subsequent judgements in the AMP does not eliminate or significantly mitigate the average AMP effect.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly confirm the original warning comparison. Added monetary incentives test an extension, rather than an original incentive finding; the method critique does not state that the original warning comparison is invalid.
